title: Red-alert rate varies eightfold across hazard types within the same feed and scale
statement: All 100 futures notarized tonight share one source (GDACS) and one two-step severity scale (Orange, Red), yet the share reaching Red differs sharply by hazard: drought 0/6 (0%), wildfire 1/20 (5%), flood 3/24 (12%), earthquake 6/30 (20%), tropical cyclone 10/20 (50%). No drought episode in the record has ever been notarized at Red; tropical cyclones are ten times more likely to appear as Red than wildfires. This is a statement about tonight's accumulated record only — it does not claim droughts are less severe in the world, only that GDACS's Orange/Red split, as recorded here, sorts hazard types very unevenly.
method: Grouped foreknown/registry.json futures by `hazard`, counted `severity` values per group. Reproducible with: python3 -c "import json,collections; f=json.load(open('foreknown/registry.json'))['futures'].values(); c=collections.defaultdict(collections.Counter); [c[x['hazard']].update([x['severity']]) for x in f]; print(dict(c))"
worth_watching_because: A single night cannot separate a real reporting pattern from a small-sample artifact (n=6 for drought, n=20 for wildfire and tropical cyclone). Not proposed as a sensor tonight for that reason — it needs a second independently-observed night before a test_rule could be written without curve-fitting to one sample.
